EntertainmentTab.title: U2 on Dolly Parton's final duet; and the 'grudge match' behind their new album
EntertainmentTab.text:
U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.

Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).

When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2009 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".

So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.

The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. (Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court.)

U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.

Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.

"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.

"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.

"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.

"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."

For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.

This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever, external since, external.

There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.

Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two, and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.

The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".

There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".

"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.

"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.

"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

During recording sessions last year, Bono told me U2 were chasing "the sound of the future". In a separate interview with Radio 2's Jo Whiley, guitarist The Edge claimed they were working on an album of "sci-fi Irish folk".

The results sure sound like U2, though.

The electronic groove of the opening track, Go (Carnaval de Luz), echoes their experimental 90s phase; while the serrated riffs of Silencio are direct descendants of 2004's Vertigo.

Parton's original lyric was about a woman trying to choose between two men but, with help from Snow Patrol's Jonny McDaid, U2 rewrote the song to address the political divisions tearing families apart.

"Brothers turn to strangers /And sons deny their name / Somebody loses either way And every heart is torn."

Parton recorded her parts in June, less than three months before she died.

"We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal," says Bono.

"That was a real shock. A shock for us because we'd been working with her, but a shock for anyone who loves music.

"I remember I was with [R.E.M. frontman] Michael Stipe in a car when the news came in, and he actually fell down and started sobbing. He just could not believe it.

"Probably the only thing that people can agree on in the entire world right now is Dolly Parton. Whether you're gay or straight or conservative or liberal, she was ready for you to fly at her show."

Another female presence shimmers on the fourth track, The Mirror Maker, which is dedicated to Catalan superstar Rosalía. Written after witnessing her spell-binding Lux tour, Bono describes the "heavens swirling" to reveal "the re-enchantment of the world".

"Normally you have to be dead or in jail for us to write a song about you," he laughs, "but she's a feminine force field. A kind of transcendent, ecstatic musician."

He wrote the song without her knowledge, phoning the singer afterwards to timidly seek her approval.

"It could have been excruciating if she really, really hated it," he grimaces. "I'd have had to pretend it was about Santa Rosalia, a saint who lived in a cave in Italy in the 17th Century."

According to producer Jacknife Lee, The Mirror Maker went through 196 different takes before U2 were happy, suggesting they haven't entirely abandoned their perfectionist streak.

"The early sessions for this album were at times super inspiring, and then really not that good at all," admits The Edge, identifying a stubborn "stick-with-it-ness" that stops them from giving up.

"This band is absolutely relentless," agrees Bono. "It's a grudge match."

"It's the most frustrating thing," Mullen Jr adds. "I'm always reminded of how incapable I am of doing all those things that other people find easy.

"It's always been a challenge for us, and that's what makes those moments when it [works] so special. That's why you keep on chasing it, and why you stay in a band."

There's more to U2's longevity than that, though. Their line-up has remained unchanged since they first formed at Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School 50 years ago. They remain friends first, and superstars second.

When we meet, in a bingo hall that hosted some of U2's formative gigs, there's a familial vibe to the whole operation.

They tease Mullen Jr for turning a hose on fans who climbed the wall of his parents' house in 1976; and chat animatedly about their musical obsessions ("every four-piece wants to be the Beatles," confesses Bono).

Those bonds have kept the band together through commercial and critical ups and downs, not to mention the life-altering injuries that forced Bono to cancel a 2010 US tour, and neck problems that prompted Mullen Jr to skip their 2023-2024 Las Vegas residency.

Doctors advised him to retire, but after a (risky) surgical intervention, he's back behind the kit – developing an entirely new playing style to avoid further damage.

His determination will be put to the test next year, when U2 embark on a massive international stadium tour, including four UK dates at London's Tottenham Hotspur Stadium next June.

The US leg will see them play some of the same venues as their friend, Ed Sheeran. So what did they make of the controversy over his recent US tour – where some venue owners pressured Sheeran into dropping his support act, Macklemore, for making pro-Palestinian comments?

"We totally support Macklemore's right as an artist to say what he wanted to say," says The Edge.

"I don't think Ed should be vilified. He was in a very difficult situation. But I commend the other young artists who decided to leave [his] tour.

"They were sticking up for an artist's right to free speech, and I think that's the issue above anything else."

He recalls several occasions where U2 themselves made risky political statements on stage.

In 1987, after Arizona's governor banned Martin Luther King Day, Bono faced death threats if he dared to play Pride (In The Name of Love) - which addresses King's assassination - in the state.

He went ahead and did it anyway, closing his eyes in anticipation of a gunshot.

"I looked up at the end of the verse and I clearly wasn't dead," he later told Mojo magazine. 'But not only that... Adam Clayton was standing in front of me."

Similarly, in 1998, the band taunted Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet during a televised concert in Santiago. At the end of the night, they invited the mothers of the victims of Pinochet's 1973 coup d'état on to the stage, who took it in turns to say the names of their children into the microphone.

"It would have been way smarter and better for us to shut up," says the Edge. "But it was artistically necessary, and we just said, 'We can't not do this'."

Reflecting further on the Macklemore controversy, he adds: "We might disagree with some of the members of the pro-Palestine movement, but we absolutely agree with the fundamentals. We absolutely agree that what's going on [in Gaza] is unconscionable and that a child's life is equally valuable, no matter what their background."

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Mullen Jr is equally forthright about the freedom to speak out.

"We, as a band, will fight for the right to speak your mind, as long as it doesn't incite violence," he says.

"Even if we disagree with it or don't like it, nobody - no billionaire, no promoter, no owner - has the right to censor anybody.

"And they will definitely not be censoring us, ever."

Like I said: U2 are at their best when they trust their instincts.

EntertainmentTab.title: Olivia Rodrigo's Christmas song sounds familiar... on purpose
EntertainmentTab.text:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo unwrapped her first-ever Christmas song on Thursday night, alongside a festive music video starring Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon.

The track, called Take Me Home (4 Christmas), finds the pop star asking her boyfriend to "show some serious commitment" by bringing her to his parents' house for the Christmas break.

As soon as it was released, fans noticed similarities to The Waitresses' 1981 festive hit Christmas Wrapping... And it turns out that was by design rather than mistake.

Chris Butler, who wrote The Waitresses' song, posted a message on Facebook, external, saying Rodrigo had contacted him to seek permission for the song; and praising her "phenomenal" writing.

"About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be 'Olivia Rodrigo'," he said. "Said she'd written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it."

Admitting he'd never heard of the pop star before, Butler said he assumed the email was a fake.

But after researching her career, he became a fan - not just of her music, but of the fact she'd hired an all-female band, and negotiated control of her master recordings.

In the end, he decided to reply to her email - and posted the text to his Facebook profile.

"If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering," he said.

"They're really sweet and flattering... even if you AREN'T you.

"If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you, I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them.

He continued: "I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you "got" my songwriting, and that you like our band."

Butler also accepted the invitation to hear Rodrigo's Christmas song, and told his followers: "Her song was/is great.

"It's going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas number one contest they have every year in the UK."

Although the song is indebted to the Waitresses' new wave and post-punk sound, Butler does not receive a writing credit on Take Me Home (4 Christmas) as it neither samples nor interpolates any of his music.

Posting on social media, Rodrigo said it was written last summer with her longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, and Amy Allen, who has previously contributed to songs by Harry Styles, Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McCrae.

Meanwhile, the Christmas jumper-tastic video, external follows the single's storyline, with SNL star Ben Marshall playing her feckless boyfriend, and Nixon starring as her prospective mother-in-law.

EntertainmentTab.title: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'
EntertainmentTab.text:
British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.

DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally".

"If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.

Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023, "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.

Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK.

It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.

Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped.

"I want to find solutions," he says.

"Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."

EntertainmentTab.title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK crowns winner as BBC axes the series
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning: This article includes spoilers for the finale of RuPaul's Drag Race UK.

After 10 weeks of toe-to-toe lip-syncs, fierce runways and shady remarks, the time has come for one queen to be named the UK's next Drag Race superstar.

For the final time on the BBC, 12 contestants were whittled down to just one after the broadcaster announced it was axing RuPaul's Drag Race UK due to budget cuts.

On Thursday night, RuPaul crowned Flesh as the series eight winner.

The London queen snatched the title from Mocha, Naya Thorn and Alik, who also made it to the final episode.

The 26-year-old was crowned by last year's winner, Bones, who is also her best friend and drag sister, with the duo performing together as Heavenly Bodies.

Speaking to BBC Newsbeat after celebrating overnight, the Soho queen says the win still feels "surreal" and she spent the whole evening "smiling, crying, and laughing".

She will be the last queen crowned on the BBC before the UK edition moves to Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

While some fans have welcomed the prospect of a new chapter for the series which might include bigger cash prizes, like in other spin-offs, others fear leaving the BBC will mean less representation for LGBTQ+ culture.

Flesh says the move to Wow could widen the range of performers and subcultures featured on the show, but worries the shift to subscription could reduce the audience for drag.

"This is where it feels slightly sadder that we're leaving the BBC because for all of the parameters that it created that limited what we could do, there was more exposure than drag has ever been given," she says.

She admits she is "concerned" about the "knock-on effect" this could have on the future of the UK drag industry, such as creating fewer opportunities for contestants.

"Without that exposure, there will be less demand and with less demand and less exposure, events won't be able to be created," she says.

Amid this concern, Flesh encourages people to connect with their local drag community and performers to consider ways they can evolve performances to bring in new audiences.

The decision to shelve the programme was announced shortly after the latest series began airing, with the BBC saying it was facing "very difficult choices" amid "significant financial pressures".

Flesh was awarded the £25,000 cash prize after impressing the judges in the final maxi challenge, which saw the last four queens perform a megamix of girl group anthems from past series.

Wrapping the show's stint on the BBC this way felt like a "really fun and tasteful way to reflect on the iconography of Drag Race UK", says Flesh, who hopes the past contestants feel "honoured".

But she reveals the final group of queens did think the "writing was on the wall" for show's future when they were asked to do the mix.

Flesh has stood out across the series as a fashion queen, bringing looks to the runway that RuPaul said would go down in the series' history.

Speaking to RuPaul and judge Michelle Visage during the final episode, Flesh said Drag Race "tells people it's not only OK to be them but it's a gift and a dream, and to be crowned the UK's next drag race superstar would be mine coming true".

She made it through the series without ever being in the bottom two and only had to lip-sync for the first time in the final when the top three queens battled it out for the win.

After Alik was eliminated, Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn performed a rendition of David Bowie's Modern Love.

EntertainmentTab.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
EntertainmentTab.text:
Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.

On Thursday, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

The broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said she was "very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt", adding that the show's budget would be reinvested in "distinctive new programming".

The Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny, made the following allegations:

One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.

Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".

Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, chair of the House of Commons culture and media committee, said the decision to axe the show "makes sense" given the review's findings and the "seriousness of the allegations".

"Reality TV contestants have often been treated as a commodity, with duty of care a slogan rather than a genuine principle. Everyone involved in producing and regulating reality TV must now learn and act," she added.

A spokesman for Ofcom said the broadcast regulator would "carefully consider the reports published today as we move to strengthen our guidance for broadcasters".

"We are clear that broadcasters have a duty of care towards members of the public who participate in their programmes."

What is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK?

The review into the show was split into two - one part examined welfare protocols on MAFS UK, and the other reported on how Channel 4 handled the allegations.

The review into welfare protocols, led by former BBC One Controller Lorraine Heggessey, concluded that some parts of the programme's format increased "the risk profile of the show".

Although she found the protocols for MAFS UK were extremely thorough and of a high standard, she said "intimacy is a key focus", and that "some elements of the show could implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate".

Heggessey made suggestions including installing CCTV in all areas of the apartments, constantly monitored by a welfare team, with panic buttons and "safe words" in place.

She concluded that, with enhancements to the existing welfare framework and adjustments to the format, it would have been reasonable to continue to produce future series of MAFS UK.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Thursday, she added that the suggested changes "would have, in lots of ways, changed both the format and the nature of the show, but would have given the kind of protection that both Channel Four and CPL would have ideally looked for to ensure the safety of all contributors".

But she added that she "completely understood" why Dogra "decided that she doesn't want to proceed with it".

The other part of the review, by law firm Clyde & Co, found that Channel 4 and CPL's welfare protocols were compliant with Ofcom's broadcasting code.

There were no findings of a breach of the code regarding the handling of issues raised at the relevant times.

But it said there were "a small number of instances" where the show's protocols had not been fully applied.

This included one incident when "some contributors contravened the Code of Conduct relating to prohibited substances but were given a first and final warning rather than being removed from the programme".

It added that Channel 4 and CPL could have undertaken a more structured longer-term review over multiple series.

The review also made recommendations for areas where the contributor welfare framework could be "further strengthened".

Dogra said welfare across all of their programmes is "a primary concern".

She said that considering the "wholesale implementation" of the recommendations "provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years".

She added that the review "did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama programme".

Billed as a "bold social experiment", Married at First Sight UK - known to many as MAFS - sees single people agree to "marry" total strangers, after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.

The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on honeymoon, before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.

The UK version, which had been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

Following the Panorama broadcast, Channel 4's chief executive Priya Dogra initially didn't apologise, although she did express her "sympathy" for those who had spoken up.

Less than 48 hours later, she changed position, telling reporters she was "deeply sorry" over the women's distress.

The impact of the Panorama progamme was swift, and sizeable.

Channel 4 launched its external review, all the episodes were taken down from its streaming service, and a major sponsor pulled out.

Married at First Sight UK usually starts airing in September, but the new series was put on hold following the revelations in the Panorama.

Ofcom has since launched an investigation, and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.

The individual is not being named. The alleged victim is also not being named; anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.

EntertainmentTab.title: Sir Tom Jones tells fans he thought life 'was over' after flu
EntertainmentTab.text:
Sir Tom Jones has told fans he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital in the US with flu.

The 86-year-old from Pontypridd spent a week at the Ronald Regan UCLA Medical Center in Los Angeles and was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of concerts.

But on Wednesday night, he was back on stage at the Greek Theatre and told the audience just how serious his "bad case of the flu" was.

"[I thought] Oh well, this is it, you've had a wonderful life, Tommy, but it's over right now," he said.

"I must say this, in the UCLA, they really did a wonderful job. So I'm here."

"[The medical staff said] What do you want to do now? I was in there for a week. And I said, 'I've got to get back on the stage'. This is where I belong. I can't live without this, believe me."

Sir Tom recently made headlines after revealing ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from The Voice UK coaching panel, having served as an coach on the singing competition since its debut in 2012.

In the latest series, and his last as a coach, he mentored Welsh singer Cate McHugh to victory.

EntertainmentTab.title: John Frieda: Celebrity hairstylist dies aged 75
EntertainmentTab.text:
British celebrity hairstylist and beauty brand entrepreneur John Frieda has died aged 75.

Frieda became a firm favourite with celebrities throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and is known to have cut hair for clients including British model Twiggy, US First Lady Jackie Kennedy and Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

He was also known for the range of hair products bearing his name, and the iconic Purdey bowl cut which he created for The New Avengers actor Joanna Lumley in 1976.

His death was announced by his hair salon in an Instagram post on Tuesday., external

"It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully ….surrounded by his family", the statement said

"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.

"Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts."

Throughout his career, Frieda worked with other famous clients including Diana, Princess of Wales, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Scarlett Johansson.

Born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951, his father was a hairdresser who owned a salon in Ealing, west London, while his grandfather had also been a Fleet Street barber.

After having gone into the family business, Frieda later joined Leonard Lewis's star-studded salon House of Leonard - famous for having created Twiggy's famous crop - becoming his assistant.

He went on to work for fashion magazines British Vogue and Harper's Bazaar.

In 1976, Frieda opened his own salon in central London which became massively successful and booked up months in advance as his reputation as an influential stylist grew.

He subsequently opened branches across the world, including in Barbados, Ibiza and Los Angeles.

In the 1990s, Frieda stepped back from cutting hair and concentrated on developing his own brand of hair products, including Frizz-Ease hair serum which he created in 1988.

His business empire grew rapidly over the following decade as it expanded into the US and across the world.

In 2002, he and his business partner Gail Federici sold the company to a Japanese conglomerate Kao for $450m (£334m).

Speaking to the British Beauty Council, external in June, Frieda gave his advice for future generation of British hairdressers.

"If you have a client in front of you, rather than thinking about the money or what you're getting from cutting their hair, just think about the action," he said.

"The reward is giving her the best haircut she's ever had. That is your reward."

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘He left the world in ruins’: the author who defied the Taliban and burning tyres to tell Alexander the Great’s epic story
EntertainmentTab.text:
He was the most powerful man in the world but he was brought down by one battle too many after a decade at the top. The story of Alexander the Great might be more than 2,000 years old, but it seems timely that a new biography of the ancient ruler won the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction just as President Trump took a battering in the US midterms. “This is a moment,” says its author Edmund Richardson, “where people are finding that there are limits to what unlimited wealth and power can do, and that humanity catches up with you, whether you like it or not. Alexander wants to transform the world – and he leaves it in ruins.”

Wearing a purple velvet jacket, purple scarf and matching socks, with a high forehead and corona of auburn curls, Richardson himself might have stepped out of an earlier age. It is hard to imagine anyone less like history’s favourite mob boss than this softly spoken professor of classics. We are having coffee at the offices of the PR company for the Baillie Gifford prize, the view of the City of London skyline from the floor to ceiling windows a reminder of 21st-century power and economics.

It would, we agree, have made the perfect backdrop for an interview with Patrick Radden Keefe, a previous winner of the £50,000 Baillie Gifford prize and the favourite this year for London Falling, a forensic investigation into the death of a teenager who falls from one of the city’s luxury skyscrapers. “I would never, ever have imagined this,” Richardson says, almost in a whisper. “I am fully expecting someone to tap me on the shoulder and say, ‘I’m so sorry, there’s been a terrible mistake, Mr Radden Keefe is waiting. You can take a coffee as you go.’”

Richardson’s exhilarating, exhaustively researched Alexander: God, King, Man is another triumph for the classics in a year when Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey stormed the box office (Alexander liked to sleep with a copy of Homer under his pillow, apparently). Like many, Richardson first encountered the figure in the pages of Alexander, Mary Renault’s 1969 fictional trilogy, when he was a boy. Critics have described his book as “part novel, part history”.

Richardson doesn’t just make the ruler of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon flesh and blood for a new generation. He also makes bold claims for his subject. “Alexander reshaped reality more profoundly than almost anyone else in history,” he writes. His expansionist campaigns might have been brutal, even by ancient standards, with his empire unravelling before his death, but for Richardson its true legacy is in the “ripple effects” that we still feel today. “It’s in the ways that Babylonian science turns up in Greece, that Greek art turns up on the borders of the Indus, that Egyptian scholarship finds its way into how we understand Homer. It’s in the world becoming far more connected.” He was antiquity’s answer to the internet.

“Alexander’s story is on this impossible scale,” he says. “This is someone who is capable of extraordinary violence and cruelty, extraordinary kindness and love.” Richardson describes the book as a “beautiful monster” to write. From Plutarch to Horrible Histories, there have been countless takes on Alexander’s story: the boy from the Macedon hills, who became king aged 20 in 336BC after his father was assassinated; marched his army into the heart of the Persian empire; had conquered much of the known world by the time he was 30, killing 1% of the population along the way; and who died “brokenhearted” in Babylon aged 32.

“Up until this book,” says Richardson, “my thing has always been writing stuff that no one reads about people no one has heard of. That’s my happy place!” His previous book, Alexandria: The Quest for the Lost City, was a biography of 19th-century archaeologist Charles Masson. But when his editor suggested he write about Alexander himself, he was horrified. “The idea of coming up against Alexander, and all of these thousands of versions of his story written by some of the people I admire the most in the world – absolute terror!”

Richardson, however, wanted to discover the real Alexander, before he became “great”. His search took him on his own decade-long adventure from the storage rooms of the British Museum in London to the catacombs of Egypt and the foothills of the Himalayas. Computer simulation and new discoveries gave him access to evidence and contemporary sources unavailable to earlier historians. But his travels back in time were interrupted by modern-day unrest. “There was a short encounter with a barricade of burning tyres,” he says, referring to a protest he stumbled upon in Cairo, while his visit to Afghanistan was abandoned after the Taliban ransacked his hotel.

“Terrible things tend to happen to people who take up papyrus or laptop to write the Alexander story,” he says. The first, Callisthenes, Aristotle’s great nephew, was crucified, according to some sources. “So for me, there was a sense of the story being something that consumes people. I felt my own fallibility as a writer, as a historian, vividly.” He also had to confront his own mortality.

Around three years ago, Richardson was diagnosed with cancer. He first had a melanoma as a teenager and “they’ve been back a couple of times since”. At this point, he was barely 40. “I was writing this book not knowing if I would be around when it was out in the world,” he says. He wasn’t even sure if he would finish it. His universe narrowed to the fluorescent lights and corridors of hospital. Writing became his way of travelling – “but to the world of ideas. The book, and the people I loved, reminded me that there was a version of myself that was less frightening.”

Although he was given the all clear, this time last year he was back in hospital after he collapsed, probably due to all the stress. When he came round the next day, two patients on his ward were handcuffed to police officers. “And there was me with my laptop and my hieroglyphs,” he laughs. It was a turning point, though. He had been struggling with the ending (“Obviously everyone dies and everything goes wrong”) but he returned to his “tangled” manuscript with “a feeling of trying to find a ray of hope where the light seemed to have gone out”.

Richardson, now 44, grew up in Bristol, the only child of two academics. His father, an American, is a mathematician; his mother, who is part-English and part-Irish, is an art historian. There were “layers upon layers” of books in the house. He went to a Bristol grammar school, where he thought he might follow his father into maths, but he couldn’t resist the ancient world.

“Obsessions are my weakness,” he says. “Even when I was a kid, I would find myself getting lost in stories and falling down rabbit holes.” He made it to Cambridge to study classics, where he was taught by Mary Beard. On a postdoctoral fellowship to Princeton, he met his fiance, “the love of my life”, the journalist and writer Yepoka Yeebo, who was studying at Columbia. They lived together in New York, before returning to London. “If there is good in what I write, it is her,” he whispers. “She makes me see the world entire, the wonder of things.”

His next subject – although his editor doesn’t know it yet – is the British Egyptologist Flinders Petrie. “I’m going back to books about people no one has ever heard of,” he says. “It’s the story of an archaeologist who, in the deserts of Egypt in 1888, thinks that he’s come up with a plan to defeat death.”

More immediately, he’s off to the BBC next, to talk more about Alexander. “It’s very strange as an academic to find people actually wanting to listen to what you say,” he jokes. “I feel so, so honoured.” Why does he think there is such interest the ancient world today? “It’s not just a story about the distant past,” he says. “We work with fragments, with ghosts, with things that have almost vanished – but that also lets us make these stories our own. There’s no such thing as the definitive book about Alexander. You know that there will be so many books after yours.”

How does he feel about his 10-year battle with Alexander ending in victory? “There have been some difficult times,” he admits. “It’s lovely to come out of that and into light.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump
EntertainmentTab.text:
La Petite Maison, in Nice, has a certain reputation as a five-star celebrity haunt. Beyoncé eats here. So do Elton John, Tom Cruise, Harry Styles and Leonardo DiCaprio, their meals presided over by the restaurant’s founder, Nicole, variously described in print as “eccentric”, “unique” and “truculent” (she’s standing by the entrance when I arrive, and suffice to say, doesn’t look like someone you’d much enjoy being on the wrong side of).

It’s enough of a celebrity haunt that the arrival of U2 – still incontrovertibly one of the biggest bands in the world 40 years after they could first reasonably have called themselves such – causes barely a murmur of interest among their fellow lunchtime diners. Then again, Bono is a regular. He was eating on the outdoor terrace the night of Nice’s terrorist attack, on Bastille Day in 2016, in which 86 people were killed. “I climbed through that window and hid under there,” he nods, pointing to a table at the rear of the restaurant. “Nicole,” he adds, “didn’t hide.”

It’s a very plush spot for a rehearsal lunch break, which is what my meeting with U2 amounts to. All the band’s members own houses nearby and the interview has been squeezed in among preparations for a secret gig at London’s Tate Modern, including songs they recorded in collaboration with Brian Eno – “to celebrate the great man and our collaborative history”, as the Edge puts it. The show, on Tuesday night, was the latest event in what is proving a packed year. There were the EPs Days of Ash and Easter Lily, the latter filled with songs of a spiritual bent, the former with righteous anger and invective variously inspired by the war in Ukraine, the genocide in Palestine – Bono recently caused uproar in Israel by comparing comments made by the country’s national security minister to Heinrich Himmler – and the Trump administration. (It arrived a month after ICE’s shooting of Renee Good, the subject of its opening track, American Obituary.)

There is also their first album of new material in nearly nine years, Carnaval de Luz – of which more later – and an accompanying world tour. And there was a performance at Dublin’s Mount Temple Comprehensive, to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Larry Mullen sticking a card on the school’s noticeboard (“drummer seeks musicians to form band”). U2 were greeted enthusiastically by an audience of current pupils waving homemade signs. Some were apparently suitably reverential: “Welcome home”; “Truly it’s a beautiful day”. Others were, perhaps, a little less so: “Which one of you is Inhaler’s dad?”; “When are Oasis on?”

Impertinent calls for them to cede the stage to the Gallaghers notwithstanding, the gig at their old school has made U2’s members think about their early days. It wasn’t so strange that they formed a band, muses Adam Clayton – it was, after all, the punk era, and plenty of other teenagers had the same idea. It was that, from the start, U2’s aims seemed slightly different. “We thought longevity for our band was an important goal,” he says, “which was the absolute opposite of the punk thing. In school in the 70s, we’d been faced with the petrol crisis, the economic crisis, worrying about what you were going to do. I think we thought: if we’ve got this thing, let’s just do it for as long as we can.”

“I remember that period when we first started to look for a record deal,” says the Edge. “We were actively impatient; we had a great level of expectation. It didn’t occur to us that this was preposterous. We were 16, 17, 18 and we expected to get a record deal. I think the clue’s in the title of the first album, Boy. It was a sort of examination of innocence and naivety, and those things are so important: they give you the sense that anything is possible, that change can happen, that you can be a huge band. It allowed us to think about global success, when there was almost no evidence that it was possible.”

What seems almost impossible is that U2 are still here, half a century later, with the same four members: there are doubtless other bands who can claim the same thing, but you struggle to think of one. That they have survived intact is down to what Bono calls “the soviet” – a democracy in which songwriting credits are always shared equally and everything is decided by committee.

Watching them interact over Madame Nicole’s butterflied prawns and pissaladière, you get a vague sense of how “the soviet” might work – occasionally, after Bono offers a long answer that digresses into quotations from books, songs and the Bible, another member of the band steps in and effectively grounds it, summarising what he’s just said in more direct terms. But nonetheless, there’s no getting around the fact that an equitable division of power is supposed to be a disastrous way to run a band. As Bruce Springsteen said when he inducted U2 into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005: “I believe they actually practise some form of democracy – toxic poison in a band’s head!”

“I think if we really understood how it worked, we’d have moved out of the rock’n’roll business and into political advice,” says Mullen. “You have to be able to go into a room and share and be open to most circumstances.”

“It’s got harder as time’s gone on,” says Bono. “Because, as Marianne Faithfull would say in situations like this: ‘Never underestimate the male ego, darling.’ Students of male psychology will tell you that as men lose power, be that physical, sexual, mental, you make up for it by flexing.” He laughs, saying that when his own father reached that point, “he started sleeping with an iron bar under his pillow”, and illustrates this with a story about U2’s peers in the late 70s Irish rock scene, the Virgin Prunes. “As an art prank, they came by one night and wrapped our car up in hankies and powder, then threw eggs when I went to the window. Da thought we were being attacked and the fucking iron bar came out and he’s off down the road chasing them. But our rehearsals rarely get to that level. Very rarely.”

Successful democracy or not, this year’s flurry of activity comes at the end of a lengthy period of turbulence for U2. Bono and the Edge’s flop Broadway musical about Spider-Man, in 2011; the misguided launch of 2014’s Songs of Innocence when they invaded everyone’s iTunes libraries; the cool reaction afforded that album and its successor, Songs of Experience; Bono suffering both a bike crash in 2014 that left him with umpteen broken bones and facial trauma, and open heart surgery two years later. There were triumphs along the way, not least the Innocence and Experience and Joshua Tree tours, which had a combined gross of $543m. But by the time U2 played their 2023-24 residency at the Las Vegas Sphere without Mullen – recovering from neck surgery that looked like it could end his drumming career – there were rumblings about the band’s future, not least within U2 themselves.

“U2 is the four members of the band,” says the Edge, firmly. “I think that doesn’t mean we would stop making music if somebody left, but I think it would be a very different kind of group. We definitely would acknowledge that it was a U2 part two, rather than the same thing. I’m not sure we’d be sitting here if Larry wasn’t ready to play.”

And yet Mullen is here, looking in impressively chiselled rude health, and U2’s new album sounds noticeably more confident and, well, U2-ish than Songs of Innocence or Songs of Experience, both of which carried the faint sense of a band struggling to work out where they fitted into the 21st-century landscape. There were clumsy lunges for pop contemporaneity – Auto-Tuned vocals, songwriter-for-hire Ryan Tedder in the credits – and moments that sounded less like U2 than they did Coldplay. “The coherent many have overpowered the transcendent,” offers Bono, carefully: by contrast, on Carnaval de Luz, the Edge says one of their aims was “to make music only U2 could make”.

It features a duet with Dolly Parton that is now the last song the ailing country star – or, as Bono calls her, “the last thing all Americans agreed on” – ever recorded. “To sing alongside her is to be somewhat embarrassed, and that’s not false modesty,” he says of the experience of duetting with a vocalist whose skills he compares to those of Pakistani Qawwali master Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. And there’s The Mirror Maker (Rosalía), a song in praise of the titular Spanish singer, replete with a falsetto vocal that mimics her operatic flourishes, which apparently required a meeting of the aforementioned soviet before it could go ahead.

“Just to fling the idea about and say: can we really do this?” says Bono. “I’ve been a fan for ages. She’s in the territory we were in – Catholicism, the saints, love for God – but it was a little bit embarrassing that she became so popular: like, great, U2 cop on to Rosalía just as she’s becoming the biggest star on the planet.” He ended up texting the singer to let her know what they had done. “I had to explain to one of her friends that I know that we were not, in fact, stalkers. But she was very humorous about it. She said, ‘I don’t have to sing on this, do I?’ And I said no, no, how on earth could we ask you to sing a song about you? That said, we got Johnny Cash to sing The Wanderer [on 1993’s Zooropa], and that was about him.”

“But it didn’t actually have his name in the title,” frowns Clayton. “It wasn’t called Johnny Cash: The Wanderer.”

The emotional tone of Carnaval de Luz is noticeably different from either of the EPs that preceded it, the anger of Days of Ash replaced by calls for community and a kind of defiant joy. “The news can’t break us,” as a song called Superficiality puts it.

“It’s not fiddling while Rome burns, it’s taking the fiddle off Nero and playing a better tune,” notes Bono, very Bono-ishly. “These divils must not control our mood.”

Bono says these are “exceptional times”. He is an activist who has never been averse to breaking bread with US politicians whose views evidently don’t align with his own. In the early 00s, he famously talked the Republican senator Jesse Helms, a virulent homophobe, into supporting funding to combat Aids. He lobbied George W Bush on debt relief for developing countries, and corralled a load of corporate suits into supporting the Product Red charity initiative. But he has been noticeably absent from the White House during the second Trump presidency: an administration that in 2025 disrupted the very Aids programme Bono helped to initiate.

“There’s a permission you need to feel to do a certain task,” he says, “and if you feel it spiritually. You feel like: I think I might be able to help here.” With the Trump administration, “I have been invited, but I know I’m not up to that, I don’t have the ability to negotiate [with them], it’s too much.” Bono says he doesn’t have “a plan, a strategy for successful action, a particular original idea I could get past them. Maybe just leave that to someone else. I don’t feel … the leading, is that the word? That thing where you think you know what to do.”

Mullen picks up the thread. “When money was taken away from Aids, from people in Africa, I think to be honest you were in a state of complete shock and dismay at what you were seeing. And these things take enormous amounts of time and energy and you can’t do everything, you can only do a certain amount.”

Is he saying he thinks this is a fundamentally different situation than what he’d encountered with right-wing politicians in previous administrations?

“Yes, I do,” says Bono. “It’s a new world. This is different. There’s a whiff, there’s a honk, and we’re all just trying to discern it. There’s a brand new dance and we do know its name,” he says, paraphrasing David Bowie’s Fashion. “It’s a little … fascistic. And it needs a different response.”

He talks about a meeting he had with Demis Hassabis, a Nobel prize-winning AI researcher. “Maybe one of the cleverest people on the planet,” who suggested that “unless there’s an exponential change in human behaviour and how we get on with each other and how we cooperate and reorganise to face the challenges of the world, like the climate crisis or whatever … we’re in deep trouble”. He says he still genuinely believes that rock music has a role to play in bringing people together, calling their upcoming tour “a no-holds-barred fight for a great night out”.

That’s despite a song on Carnaval de Luz called The Greatest Show on Earth, which you could take as a eulogy for U2’s imperial phase in the 80s and 90s, or for pop’s once-central, now-diminished role in culture. “We were once the greatest show on earth,” he sings, a line which apparently caused some consternation among U2’s ranks.

“Everyone was going: ‘You’re not going to sing that, are you?’,” he laughs. “Edge was saying: ‘How about: we could still be the greatest show on earth?’ Adam said: ‘What about: I think we’re the greatest show on earth?’ But I know how I feel when I sing it. The feeling of grasping that nettle – look what might have been – gives you hope.”

That time, he says, he overrode the objections of the soviet and got his own way. But it happens a lot less than you’d think, and perhaps that’s for the best. “I genuinely fantasise that one day these lads will actually just do what they’re told, but at this point, I’m giving up on that fantasy,” the Edge smiles, as U2 head for the rehearsal room. “I just don’t think it’s going to happen. And thank God, because if they started doing what they’re told, there’d be an absolutely shite album.”

Carnaval de Luz is released 13 November via Island. U2’s world tour begins 23 February at Estadio GNP Seguros, Mexico City, and includes three dates at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, London, 18-22 June

This article was updated on 6 November 2026 to correctly attribute three quotes to the Edge which were previously attributed to Bono: “To make music only U2 could make”, “I remember that period …” and “I genuinely fantasise that one day …”.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘I’m never going to be bloody Robert De Niro!’: Rob Brydon, the most chipper man on TV
EntertainmentTab.text:
‘I’m a nice person, you know,” says Rob Brydon, as I met him in a basement green room of the BBC, where probably nobody with such a mellow ego has ever sat. “I am a people-pleaser. That’s who I am.” It’s an unnecessary clarification – at 61, he’s been nice on TV, as himself and in character, for most of our adult lives.

We’re here to talk about his new six-parter, Bill’s Included, but his character in it, the eponymous Bill, is such a distillation of pure Rob Brydon that it’s (accidentally, he says) a celebration of his entire career. As the show opens, Bill has just been left by his wife, who’s run off with the gardener. At no point does he ever fire the guy – “I like him!” – but otherwise, his life is completely upended. The utterly plausible cocktail of his civic mindedness and howling loneliness drives him to take in four lodgers, local university students.

The opening moments, before he gets his young super-woke crew, are so powerfully reminiscent of Marion and Geoff that it’s like being whacked around the head and given a hot chocolate at the same time by the year 2000. The hugely funny and poignant series was Brydon’s breakthrough sitcom, the first he wrote himself (with Hugo Blick), based on a character he’d created at college – Keith, a taxi driver, speaking straight to a dashboard camera about a marriage that, the viewer realises, has been toast for ages. “I’m so thick,” Brydon says now. “It’s only when watching Bill’s Included that I went: ‘Oh, it’s got a bit of a Marion and Geoff vibe.’ Honestly, I swear to you, that hadn’t occurred to me. You don’t think about your own stuff. That’s 26 years ago!”

Steve Coogan was one of the executives on Marion and Geoff, and has been badgering Brydon to do more character comedy ever since. “I fobbed him off for years, then we made a taster of this landlord-and-students idea a few years ago, but it wasn’t right. I was too creepy.” Surely not … “I was, I was creepy, and I didn’t realise it! It was just me as a middle-aged guy, going: ‘Come in, have a sit down,’” – he does an impression of his most mellifluous and ingratiating Welsh timbre, and he’s right, it’s incredibly creepy – before snapping back to his regular voice.

Brydon and Coogan’s creative entanglement has been fruitful: 24 Hour Party People, about Factory Records in Manchester in the late 80s/early 90s – Brydon had a small part as a caustic naysayer who doesn’t like the music, Coogan played the legend Tony Wilson, head of the label. Then, Cock and Bull Story, in which they both brought the atmosphere, playing themselves, sort-of, as two egotistical actors scrapping with each other, failing to make a film about a book, Tristram Shandy, failing to become a novel. The genius of that film is all in the control: they caper about but pull it back from slapstick; it’s knowing but not arch. Seeing Brydon and Coogan mess about on set gave director Michael Winterbottom the idea for The Trip, whose Northern Lights series – its fifth – is coming soon.

When the pair first met in 1997ish, it was at a Holiday Inn in Reading. Brydon was in an improv group with the solidly magnificent Julia Davis, along with Ruth Jones, who he was also at school with, and they’d all been to the Hexagon to see Coogan, who “was already at his first peak. He was in the West End with The Man Who Thinks He’s It, he’d won a million Baftas already, he was doing what I wanted to do at the time, which is character comedy,” Brydon remembers.

“He’d started out in voiceovers, he was the same age as me, so I could see all these parallels between us.” I can’t help but remark that people, if they meet a peer they really admire, sometimes don’t like that person very much. “What, envy and stuff like that?” says Brydon, taken aback. “I can imagine that sort of person, but I can’t imagine me being like that. Envy, brute rage, competitiveness? I’m none of those things. I just look at him and think: ‘Great. Isn’t he good?’ One of the hardest things in The Trip is when Michael wants me to ridicule his career. He’s got a brilliant career!”

Brydon’s career isn’t exactly a Harrison Ford-level wilderness-to-stardom tale; he had work in improv, doing voiceovers and radio panel shows before Human Remains in 2000, when he was 35. But that blistering two-hander with Julia Davis, in which they play a variety of miserable couples, landed the same year as Marion and Geoff, and Brydon’s forte was unarguable: character comedy in which he is defiantly uncool, self-deluding and in a variety of luckless scenarios. He can effortlessly carry a show, but is just as memorable in an ensemble. His tightly wound Uncle Bryn is the performance people can’t let drop, “more or less every day, someone will come up to me and tell me how much they love Gavin & Stacey. There’s a real affection for it.”

Bill’s Included is his first show since Gavin & Stacey’s epic finale, and the camera’s on him almost constantly. His relationship with the four students, Christian (Dylan Brady), Hettie (Ada Player), James (Harry Baxendale) and Zahra (Yasmin Al-Khudhairi) starts off as a broad clash of the generations. They’re noisy, he’s fussy, and whenever they use their buzzwords – checking their privilege, trauma bonding, finding a safe space – Bill says naive, delighted things, such as: “These are the kinds of nuggets I’m going to get from you, like truffles.”

“I think that’s quite an authentic thing, someone of his age, his personality, would feel,” says Brydon. Quite fast, it becomes affectionate. “He starts off calling them the students, and by episode three, he’s saying: ‘I’ve got to go and do a thing for the kids.’ They’re not my kids! But I like to be needed.” It may sound low-stakes, but his heart is so painfully close to the surface, and the peril of some Dr Marten-ed youngster stamping on it by accident sets up intense emotional jeopardy.

Often the laughs feel ripped out of you, sheer exuberant relief that no one got hurt – like the feeling of being at a circus, except instead of tigers, you’re being entertained by suburban manners and wounded middle-aged pride. “I am what I am,” he says at that “suburban” word. “My world is not the world of the agent provocateur, activist, disruptor. That’s not me. I’m riding the horse in the direction that it’s travelling. That’s a phrase, isn’t it?” I’ve never heard it – maybe it’s Welsh, I suggest? “It’s probably from a self-help book, isn’t it?”

To stick with the phrase, few could have predicted that the horse he’s riding – whether on The Trip, Gavin & Stacey or Would I Lie to You? – would travel for so long. These are, or were, all decades-long shows, yet when Brydon describes The Trip taking shape, it sounds like that episode of Seinfeld where Jerry and George go to see some TV bigwigs to pitch a show about nothing. “Michael [Winterbottom] said: ‘Six half-hours, no script really, and different restaurants.’ I said to him: ‘You’d be lucky if you get one good half-hour.’ I was very wrong.”

From the first episode, The Inn at Whitewell, in 2010, it is plain that the idea is dynamite, but very weird dynamite. Between the squabbling, the self-aggrandisement and the impressions, you can understand why it’s funny, but the depth of feeling catches you unawares. Even by series four, you still can’t figure out why it’s as moving as it is. “How [Winterbottom] makes those shows, he doesn’t cut to comic rhythms, he has storytelling rhythms, so when we saw the cuts of the first series, it was quite jarring. He’s quite pure, Michael. He isn’t manipulative of his audience, whereas a comedian, all you’re doing is manipulating your audience.” Even after 16 years, Brydon still hasn’t turned into a food snob. “We had whale and stuff, in Scandinavia. It’s a bit like chicken.”

If you think The Trip’s been going a long time, Would I Lie to You? is now in its 19th series. “A lot of people say they watch it before going to bed. It puts them in a nice frame of mind. If you watch that show, you think the world is an agreeable place, where people get on with each other.” His nice-guy shtick is surely parodic, I decide, though he says, no, he can do villainy if he wants to, it just doesn’t do it for him. “There was a while when I thought: ‘If I host a show like Would I Lie to You?, I’ll never be taken seriously as an actor.’ But then I thought: ‘Look, I’m never going to be bloody Robert De Niro anyway, so let’s just do it.’ I think the fragmented media landscape is a gift to someone like me. There were people in Barbie – I had a tiny part in that – who didn’t even know I was an actor.”

If he sounds philosophical, almost Buddhist-ly – without front, or certainly without professional puffed-up-ness – that’s because “people always look at careers in a vacuum, and they’re not, because my life is not my career. My life is my home, my family, my friends. I’ve got five children! Katie’s 31 and George is 15. So I’ve never been in that place where I could go to Atlanta and make the X Men versus the B Men.” He’d take a second season of Bill’s Included, for sure; he’d love that. But, he says, “I don’t think your career is your greatest source of happiness. Maybe it’s from being divorced – this is my second marriage – and I’ve worked out where I’m happiest. And it’s being in the garden, with friends and in nature.”

Bill’s Included starts on 20 November on BBC One at 9.30pm.

EntertainmentTab.title: Marilyn Monroe is a magnetic misfit in Speculations, a spicy conspiracy drama full of bombshells
EntertainmentTab.text:
A smartly dressed woman hammers away at an old-style typewriter in a drawing room. She is the real-life American journalist and conspiracy theorist Dorothy Kilgallen (Janie Dee) and bears the gimlet-eyed look of Angela Lansbury in Murder, She Wrote.

Torben Betts’s play could be called Marilyn, She Wrote. It is the 1960s, Marilyn Monroe has been found dead in her bed and Kilgallen thinks both John F Kennedy and his brother Robert F Kennedy (Jolyon Coy) had something to do with it. Her investigations form part of an unpublished book which suggests links between a political cover-up and underworld crime that, she argues, led to Monroe’s death aged 36.

Kilgallen receives a threatening phone call from a stalker just as the babysitter, Flo (Gloria Obianyo), arrives. She confides in Flo and the play is shaped around their conversations, which snap to slickly enacted flashbacks of Monroe (Natalie Dunne) in her bedroom with RFK, as well as scenes of JFK’s killer, Lee Harvey Oswald (Joseph Potter), in a bar with criminal mastermind Carlos Marcello (Ferdy Roberts).

It helps that Flo is a wannabe journalist, whom Kilgallen instantly takes under her wing, and that she is African American, so sees the Kennedys as vital forces for good in the civil rights movement. But it is still too convenient a plot device that someone as shrewd as Kilgallen would explain all her theories to a complete stranger.

Director Trevor Nunn creates a smoothly oiled production nonetheless, eliciting strong performances from the cast which never seem like tacky imitations. The standout highlight is Dunne. Monroe has been played so many times that any portrayal runs the risk of cliched impersonation but Dunne is variously dishevelled, vulnerable, angry and unglamorous yet able to turn on the allure. At her most upset she appears like Monroe in her exposing final performance in The Misfits.

Lee Newby’s set design does its own transformative thing, rotating elegantly between timeframes. But all the machinery seems to try too hard to paste over the play’s limitations. It feels static as people talk out their theories and grudges.

As far as Monroe conspiracy theories go, Kilgallen’s was surely explosive then but has little new in it now. The less familiar bit here is Oswald’s connection to Marcello and Oswald’s own assassin, Jack Ruby, as well as questions around the death of Kilgallen herself in 1965, which this play leaves abruptly hanging. One speculation too few?

GeneralTab.text:

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

GeneralTab.title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
GeneralTab.text:
European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.

On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.

It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ, evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.

The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week, in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".

A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.

France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.

No explosives have been found on any planes as of Friday.

As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.

Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.

In a statement, gardaí (Irish police) said they were "aware of a threat made against media organisations here and in Europe".

While no link has been established between the threats against airlines and media outlets, the Irish government has warned it is a "likely coordinated campaign of disruption".

In a statement, it said: "Hoax threats such as these cause fear, distress and disruption to people going about their daily lives and activities; they achieve no positive purpose whatsoever. It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralised or co-ordinated effort.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin described the situation as "worrying" and added his government's first priority was the safety of the Irish public.

"Yesterday, there appeared to be coordinated efforts to disrupt air travel," he said.

Martin told RTÉ it was not yet known if the threats had come from individuals or if it was a "coordinated attack" but said they were being taken seriously.

Ireland is scheduled to host two high-profile European Union meetings in Dublin next week.

Broadcaster Sky confirmed it had received a security threat, hours after RTÉ had evacuated its building.

The broadcaster, which is owned by Comcast, said in a statement read by a presenter on its news channel that the broadcaster had "carried out a security assessment and reported the matter to the relevant authorities".

"The safety and security of our colleagues is our primary concern, and we are working closely with authorities to ensure our people and operations remain secure."

Friday's disruption comes after the Russian extremist group "Male State", named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, denied any link to the false warnings.

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"

GeneralTab.title: Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
GeneralTab.text:
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.

But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.

While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.

Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.

However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.

The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.

Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

Atmospheric disturbances can cause the air high up to start warming which then makes the vortex winds weaken. This sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) can eventually lead to the strong westerlies reversing into easterly winds.

In the following days and weeks these changes can alter the position of the jet stream, increasing the chance of a blocked weather pattern where it can become drier with a colder northerly or easterly wind bringing Arctic air in.

It can also boost the possibility of snow, especially in eastern UK.

If the winds continue to weaken and end up reversing as forecast, this will be known as a major SSW event.

Jeff Knight, lead climate scientist from the Met Office, told the BBC: "It would appear to be the earliest on record looking back over the 75 years we've been observing…with most experts agreeing this is a very unusual event."

The current earliest major SSW event occurred on 28 November in 1969 and 2025.

Reasons for why we're seeing such an early event is not clear. It could be just part of the variability of our weather patterns.

But we also know in a "normal" El Niño year, this can typically bring a weakening of the polar vortex towards the end of winter.

While the warmer waters of the Pacific in an El Niño directly disrupt the weather around tropical areas, pulses of energy in the atmosphere, known as planetary waves, can cause disturbances even at polar regions.

These waves can push the polar vortex out of position and break the circulation up.

With the current record El Niño taking us into uncharted territory in terms of disruption to worldwide weather patterns, Knight suggested it could have "helped load the dice for this SSW event. However, because this is so rare, there's not enough evidence".

A link between a strong El Niño and early onset of a SSW event is unclear and will need further research.

Long-range forecasts issued by the Met Office show that the UK was more likely to see a stormy start to winter, followed by a colder spell to end winter. This is consistent with expectations from an El Niño pattern.

However, this unusually early SSW event was not widely expected.

Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, meteorologist at the University of Reading, said: "The typical response to a SSW is for colder and drier conditions over Europe and the UK."

"Because we haven't seen a SSW event quite like this before, it is harder to anticipate a cold spell at the moment."

One reason is the timing.

The Arctic is not yet as cold as it becomes later in winter, with the polar vortex itself having only recently developed.

Any influence it may have on weather patterns could be weaker than during a mid-winter disruption.

And because the air isn't at mid-winter temperatures yet it means cold and snowy weather for the UK is far from guaranteed.

GeneralTab.title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
GeneralTab.text:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.

Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.

SpaceX and Tesla shares, which were also hammered on Thursday, saw more mixed gains, up more than 6% and nearly 5% respectively.

Chipmakers AMD and Micron both dropped by more than 17% on Thursday, but AMD shares had risen by about 12% on Friday while Micron was up more than 8%.

However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse on Friday.

The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.

In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.

In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.

"While no-one knows what happens next, it's clear that we've just seen a significant shift in market sentiment," he said.

"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

The market fluctuations come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.

A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.

US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".

However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.

Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.

"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.

"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."

He said people were watching firms come into their communities and build data centres while their own energy costs were going up, and those companies "have to be better neighbours".
